Approach to Cancer Screening and Surveillance Testing 

difficulty obtaining an adequate sample. Cervical cancer growth is slow 
and can take 10 to 30 years, and there is a possibility of spontaneous 
regression of low-grade cervical lesions in older adults.353 In addition, pap 
smears are associated with high anxiety and psychological distress. Data 
are also lacking to demonstrate any benefit in prostate cancer screening 
for patients >75 years. For patients aged 55 to 74 years, the U.S. PLCO 
trial of over 75,000 patients found no benefits,357 although younger 
patients with no comorbidities showed reduction in prostate cancer-
specific mortality rates with screening.358 

Hence, routine cancer screening should be performed on older adult 
patients after careful consideration of their overall life expectancy. If the 
patient’s life expectancy is ≤10 years, the patient is unlikely to benefit from 
routine cancer screening and more likely to experience immediate harms 
and distress. Thus, cancer screening should be stopped for such patients. 
If the patient’s life expectancy is ≥10 years, the patient’s goals and values 
must be consistent with wanting treatment if the cancer is detected to 
warrant continuation of routine screening.353 

“Surveillance testing” refers to routine assessment (in the absence of 
symptoms or abnormal physical examination findings) for recurrence or 
new primary cancers of the same type as the cancer survivor’s prior 
cancer(s) beyond routine history and physical examination. (Note that 
diagnostic evaluation is recommended for any patient with symptoms or 
signs suspicious for cancer recurrence on history or physical examination.) 
If the patient’s life expectancy is <5 years, they are unlikely to benefit from 
routine surveillance testing. The NCCN Panel recommends stopping 
routine surveillance testing for these patients in the absence of symptoms 
or findings on physical examination. If the patient’s life expectancy is ≥5 
years, the patient’s goals and values must be consistent with wanting 
treatment should cancer recurrence be detected, the health status should 

Cancer screening refers to screening for new primary cancers that are 
different than the cancer survivor’s prior cancer. The older adults with 
cancer often have multiple chronic conditions that could decrease their life 
expectancy.352 Although screening older adults could be beneficial in 
detecting cancers at early stages to allow for early intervention strategies, 
one major downside is overdiagnosis and treatment of cancers that might 
not have caused any symptoms during the patient’s lifetime.353 Harms of 
screening relevant to older adults include fatigue from tests, discomfort, 
side effects, harms of procedure after-care, and distracting/time 
consuming. Moreover, the direct benefits of cancer screening are less 
evident specifically for this population since the RCTs of screening rarely 
include older age groups.352 There is some evidence to support routine 
screening for the following cancers (although evidence in older individuals 
is limited): breast, colorectal, and lung cancer. In a retrospective cohort 
study with 5186 patients with breast cancer aged ≥65 years, mammogram 
screening of breast cancer was associated with reduction in risk of death 
for all patients with mild to moderate comorbidities; however, those with 
severe or multiple comorbidities showed no improvement in OS.354 The 
American Cancer Society recommends mammography in older patients 
who have a life expectancy of ≥10 years, as it is unlikely to benefit those 
with less than a 10-year life expectancy. Screening decisions among 
patients aged ≥75 years should be made according to overall health and 
patient preferences.355 Several trials have shown benefits of CRC 
screening such as sigmoidoscopy, fecal occult blood testing, and CT 
colonography and/or colonoscopy in older patients in reducing CRC-
specific mortality rates.356 However, colonoscopy was associated with 
serious adverse events in asymptomatic persons including perforations 
and bleeding and is not recommended for persons with less than a 10-
year life expectancy or those aged ≥85 years. There is limited or no 
evidence to support screening for cervical cancer in older people. False-
positive of abnormal pap smear is common in older patients due to

Assessing the Needs of the Caregiver 

be appropriate, and individualized, shared decision-making should be 
engaged when determining the need for routine surveillance testing. 

Older adults with cancer commonly require supportive care due to 
comorbidities, and 63% of home care for these individuals is provided by 
informal caregivers, such as a family member.363,364 Caregivers of older 
adults tend to be of a more advanced age with the average age being 63 
to 66 years.360 Additionally, caregivers may also have comorbidities that 
could affect their function as a caregiver.361,362 

The benefits of cancer screening and routine surveillance testing are likely 
to exceed the harms of screening if the patient’s risk of cancer is higher 
than average (eg, genetic cancer syndrome, prior exposures such as 
radiation or chemotherapy) and if life expectancy is sufficient (>5 years). 
The harm of screening and surveillance testing will outweigh the benefit in 
the setting of significant comorbidities, which can limit the ability to 
conduct the test (eg, colonoscopy in the setting of significant cardiac or 
lung disease) or impact ability to treat cancer if detected. For example, 
patients with favorable-subtype breast cancers treated with endocrine 
therapy carry a lower risk of recurrence/new primaries compared to 
similar-aged patients with no history of breast cancer, and thus are not 
likely to benefit from routine surveillance testing. 359 

Considerations for Caregivers of Older Adults with 
Cancer 

Along with more advanced age and comorbidities, many caregivers of 
older adults experience substantial physical and psychological stress 
associated with their role, making it critical to also assess the well-being of 
the caregiver. This can be done by exploring their confidence in providing 
care as well as determining their need for additional resources and/or 
support. This is especially true as many caregivers will not openly express 
their struggles. The Panel recommends use of the Zarit Burden Interview, 
Caregiver Reaction Scale, or Caregiver Self-Assessment Questionnaire to 
determine if the caregiver has a willingness and ability to assume care 
responsibilities. These responsibilities should also be reassessed 
periodically as the needs of the patient evolve. 

Caregivers of older adults with cancer typically play critical roles in 
decision-making surrounding treatment and end-of-life care as well as 
provide essential support in daily living, social needs, practical assistance 
(eg, transportation, meal preparation), physical care, and financial 
management. Patient advocacy, which includes helping patients navigate 
medical decisions and coordination of their care with clinicians and 
insurers, is also a major function that the caregiver can serve for an older 
adult with cancer.360-362 Thus, the Panel recommends that caregiver status 
of the patient should be determined, and if the patient does not have a 
caregiver, referral to social work is encouraged. If a patient does have a 
caregiver, it is necessary to determine if the caregiver has an 
understanding of what may be asked of them, including assessing 
availability, willingness, and burden. 

The Zarit Burden Interview (also known as the Zarit Scale of Caregiver 
Burden) is the most widely used instrument to measure caregiver burden. 
Originally, it was designed to have 29 items but subsequent adaptations 
led to its reduction to a short 12-item version and 4-item screening 
version, which correlate with the longer versions.365,366 Additional 
assessment tools for caregiver stress and burden that can be used include 
the Caregiver Strain Index,367 Caregiver Reaction Scale,368 and the 
Caregiver Self-Assessment Questionnaire, which was developed and 
tested by the American Medical Association. Assessment of caregiver 
coping should also be conducted with tools such as the Revised Scale for 
Caregiving Self-Efficacy369 and the Perceived Support Scale,370 as well as 
the Cultural Justification for Caregiving Scale.371 

MS-32

pages.title: Older Adult Oncology
pages.text:
Strategies for improving the support of caregivers can include education 
and training as well as involving caregivers in treatment decisions, which 
can aid in improving the care plan so that it aligns with both the wishes of 
the patient and their family. Additionally, it is recommended that caregivers 
seek support through community or professional support services such as 
licensed social workers or non-medical home care services such as 
housekeeping, meal preparation, or transportation. Spiritual care should 
also be considered for some families. Physicians can direct caregivers to 
the toolkit that is provided by the Family Caregiver Alliance, which 
provides many resources to family caregivers of adults with a wide range 
of impairments. 

Summary 

The goal of the NCCN Guidelines for Older Adult Oncology is to assist 
clinicians in providing evidence-based care that addresses the unique 
issues faced by older adults with cancer. Implementing GA-driven care 
along with consideration of the common treatment side effects described 
here can ultimately enhance treatment decision-making, tolerance, 
outcomes, and improve QOL for older adults with cancer. The Panel 
recommends that cancer treatment for older adults be individualized 
based on the nature of the disease, the physiologic status of the patient, 
and the patient’s values and goals with concurrent consideration for the 
needs of the patient’s caregiver. These Guidelines will continue to be 
updated as recommendations evolve in order to provide a roadmap to 
assist providers in tailoring their clinical practice to provide the best care 
possible to this vulnerable patient population.

lines: DEFINITION AND PURPOSE

nodes.text: Definition of the Older Adult Oncology Population • There is no chronologic age threshold to define an older adult. The guidelines herein focus on physiologic age and function to define the older adult oncology population. (Note: Some consider individuals aged ≥65 years to be older adults, as this is the usual age of eligibility for Medicare benefits.)
lines: Definition of the Older Adult Oncology Population
• There is no chronologic age threshold to define an older adult. The guidelines herein focus on physiologic age and function to define the
older adult oncology population. (Note: Some consider individuals aged ≥65 years to be older adults, as this is the usual age of eligibility for
Medicare benefits.)

nodes.text: Purpose of the NCCN Guidelines for Older Adult Oncology • There are unique issues to consider when caring for an older adult with cancer. • The biologic characteristics of certain cancers and their responsiveness to therapy may be different in older patients compared to their younger counterparts. • The psychologic and psychosocial changes associated with aging may impact an older adult’s ability to tolerate cancer therapy and should be considered in the treatment decision-making process. See NCCN Guidelines for Distress Management. • Advanced age alone should not be the only criterion to preclude effective treatment that could improve quality of life (QOL) or lead to a survival benefit in older patients. • Multidisciplinary team management, patient-specific treatment approach with shared decision-making, and palliative/supportive care for symptom management should be an integral part of cancer care in older adults. See NCCN Guidelines for Supportive Care and NCCN Guidelines for Palliative Care. • These age-related issues form the basis for the development of NCCN Guidelines for Older Adult Oncology that address special considerations in older patients with cancer.

nodes.text: General Considerations • Patient's values and goals should be assessed in context with life expectancy; comorbidities; cognitive, functional, psychologic/ psychosocial, and nutritional status; aggressiveness of the disease; and treatment approach (OAO-3). • There are data to suggest correlation between low social support and a higher risk for mortality. In patients with low levels of social support, consider referral to social work and/or case management to explore home supports and community resources. • Offer a shared decision-making tool/framework to guide treatment decisions. • Multidisciplinary team management, patient-specific treatment approach with shared decision-making, and palliative/supportive care for symptom management should be an integral part of cancer care in older adults. See NCCN Guidelines for Supportive Care and NCCN Guidelines for Palliative Care. • Older adult cancer care is complex; thus, use of multidisciplinary care teams and testing of different models of care delivery can be strategies for efficient care delivery. • Observation may be an appropriate approach in particular clinical scenarios, and may align with patient's preference. • Age-Friendly Health Systems provides a set of four evidence-based elements of high-quality care to all older adults known as the 4Ms. What Matters: Care is aligned with individual values, goals, and preferences. Mobility: Move safely and maintain function Medication: Treatment is necessary and non-redundant Mentation: Prevent, identify, treat, and manage dementia, depression, and delirium Specific Considerations by Treatment Type
lines: General Considerations
• Patient's values and goals should be assessed in context with life expectancy; comorbidities; cognitive, functional, psychologic/
psychosocial, and nutritional status; aggressiveness of the disease; and treatment approach (OAO-3).
• There are data to suggest correlation between low social support and a higher risk for mortality. In patients with low levels of social support,
consider referral to social work and/or case management to explore home supports and community resources.
• Offer a shared decision-making tool/framework to guide treatment decisions.
• Multidisciplinary team management, patient-specific treatment approach with shared decision-making, and palliative/supportive care for
symptom management should be an integral part of cancer care in older adults. See NCCN Guidelines for Supportive Care and NCCN
Guidelines for Palliative Care.
• Older adult cancer care is complex; thus, use of multidisciplinary care teams and testing of different models of care delivery can be
strategies for efficient care delivery.
• Observation may be an appropriate approach in particular clinical scenarios, and may align with patient's preference.
• Age-Friendly Health Systems provides a set of four evidence-based elements of high-quality care to all older adults known as the 4Ms.
What Matters: Care is aligned with individual values, goals, and preferences.
Mobility: Move safely and maintain function
Medication: Treatment is necessary and non-redundant
Mentation: Prevent, identify, treat, and manage dementia, depression, and delirium
Specific Considerations by Treatment Type

nodes.text: • Chronologic age is not the primary consideration for surgical risk; all older adults undergoing surgery should undergo an assessment for components of frailty including comorbidities, cognition, mobility, functional status, and nutrition. For patients who are at high risk with multimorbidities and complex health conditions, consider multidisciplinary input with geriatric expertise. • The American College of Surgeons (ACS) Geriatric Surgery Verification (GSV) Program provides a framework for hospitals to take an interdisciplinary approach to continuously optimize surgical care for older adults. The GSV Program includes 32 standards to improve surgical care for older adults with an emphasis on goals of care and shared decision-making, assessment of geriatric-specific vulnerabilities (eg, cognition, mobility), and interdisciplinary postoperative care. • The ACS National Surgical Quality Improvement Program (NSQIP) Surgical Risk Calculator includes both geriatric-specific predictors and geriatric-specific outcomes; the ACS NSQIP Surgical Risk Calculator can be a useful tool for sharing patient-specific predicted outcomes after surgery and facilitating a more informed discussion regarding risks of surgery. • Delirium is often preventable and the most common postoperative complication in older adults; the American Geriatrics Society (AGS) practice guideline on postoperative delirium in older adults covers the topic areas of delirium risk factors, diagnosis and screening, prevention, medical evaluation, and pharmacologic treatment. See OAO-F 2 of 4. • The surgical plan can be altered as necessary to consider nonsurgical or less morbid options.

diagnosis and screening, prevention, medical evaluation, and pharmacologic treatment. See OAO-F 2 of 4.
• The surgical plan can be altered as necessary to consider nonsurgical or less morbid options.
Surgery

nodes.text: • Improvements in RT techniques including intensity-modulated RT (IMRT), image-guided RT (IGRT), and stereotactic ablative radiotherapy (SABR) have improved the tolerability and therapeutic ratio of RT in older adults. • Considerations of older patients undergoing RT should be informed by the benefits versus risks based on the anatomic site being radiated and the dose/fractionation chosen. Chronologic age by itself should not exclude patients from evaluation for curative RT. • Use caution with concurrent chemoradiation therapy. Dose or sequence modification of chemotherapy or chemoradiation, additional supportive services, and more frequent monitoring may be necessary. See disease- specific NCCN Guidelines for Treatment by Cancer Type. • Hypofractionation and SABR may be considered to decrease the number of treatments, especially in patients who are frail and/or less mobile. • Local ablative RT should be considered as an adjunct or alternative therapy in older adults.

nodes.text: • Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has been shown to be an effective therapeutic option for older adults with similar response rates as younger adults, and age should not be a contraindication for using these therapies. • Cellular therapies come with a range of toxicities for older adults. Older adults, especially those who are frail, may have a higher incidence of neurologic toxicities and require close monitoring (NCCN Guidelines for the Management of CAR T-Cell and Lymphocyte Engager-Related Toxicities).

nodes.text: Monitor for symptomatic or asymptomatic congestive heart failure (CHF). • Caution with use of anthracyclines; consider alternative treatment dosing schedule or treatment as appropriate per disease site (NCCN Guidelines for Treatment by Cancer Type). • Caution with use of trastuzumab (among patients with normal left ventricular ejection fraction [LVEF]; risk factors for CHF include older age, receipt of an anthracycline-based regimen, baseline LVEF of 50%–54%, coronary artery disease, hypertension, and weekly trastuzumab administration) (see SCARDIO-1, SCARDIO-2, and SCARDIO-3 in the NCCN Guidelines for Survivorship).

Insomnia (OAO-G)

nodes.text: Benzodiazepines or other sedative-hypnotics should not be used as first-line treatment for insomnia in older adults; non-pharmacologic methods such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and lifestyle modifications are preferred (see Sleep Disorders in NCCN Guidelines for Survivorship).

nodes.text: High-dose steroids for the management of treatment-related toxicities must be used with caution in older patients as it may worsen other comorbidities or cognitive function. • NCCN Guidelines for the Management of Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor-Related Toxicities • NCCN Guidelines for the Management of CAR T-Cell and Lymphocyte Engager-Related Toxicities

is_candidate_for_cancer_specific_treatme.criteria: considering the patient's overall life expectancy
is_candidate_for_cancer_specific_treatme.definition: Clinician judgement, considering the patient's overall life expectancy, that the patient is a candidate for cancer-specific treatment.

has_decision_making_capacity.criteria: Patients must have the ability to: • Understand the relevant information about proposed cancer-specific diagnostic tests or treatment options • Appreciate their situation (including their underlying values and current medical situation) • Use reason to make a decision • Communicate a consistent choice
has_decision_making_capacity.definition: Clinician judgement that the patient can understand relevant information about proposed options, appreciate their situation, use reason to decide, and communicate a consistent choice.

values_goals_consistent_with_cancer_spec.criteria: Are the patient's values and goals consistent with wanting cancer-specific treatment?
values_goals_consistent_with_cancer_spec.definition: Clinician judgement that the patient's values and goals are consistent with wanting cancer-specific treatment.

concerns_tolerating_cancer_specific_trea.criteria: Are there any concerns about the patient's ability to tolerate cancer-specific treatment? Concerns can come from the patient, family, or clinician and can be related to the patient's performance status and/or comorbidities.
concerns_tolerating_cancer_specific_trea.definition: Clinician judgement that there are concerns about the patient's ability to tolerate cancer-specific treatment.

geriatric_screen_result.definition: Result of the geriatric screening tools administered to the patient.

geriatric_assessment_abnormalities_prese.definition: Whether the geriatric assessment identified abnormalities that require treatment or intervention.

alternate_treatment_reduces_toxicity_acc.criteria: Are there alternate treatment options that would reduce toxicity to an acceptable level?
alternate_treatment_reduces_toxicity_acc.definition: Clinician judgement that alternate treatment options exist which would reduce toxicity to an acceptable level.

tox_gi_related.definition: Patient has or is at risk of gastrointestinal toxicity (diarrhea, constipation, nausea or vomiting) from cancer-specific treatment.

tox_mucositis.definition: Patient has or is at risk of mucositis from cancer-specific treatment.

tox_bone_marrow_suppression.definition: Patient has or is at risk of bone marrow suppression from cancer-specific treatment.

tox_infection_immunosuppression.definition: Patient has or is at risk of infection or immunosuppression from cancer-specific treatment.

tox_neurotoxicity.definition: Patient has or is at risk of neurotoxicity from cancer-specific treatment.

tox_falls.definition: Patient has or is at risk of falls related to cancer-specific treatment.

tox_cardiac.definition: Patient has or is at risk of cardiac toxicity from cancer-specific treatment.

tox_renal.definition: Patient has or is at risk of renal toxicity from cancer-specific treatment.

tox_insomnia.definition: Patient has or is at risk of insomnia related to cancer-specific treatment.

tox_fatigue.definition: Patient has or is at risk of fatigue related to cancer-specific treatment.

tox_irae.definition: Patient has or is at risk of immune-related adverse events from cancer-specific treatment.

tox_reduced_appetite_weight_loss.definition: Patient has reduced appetite or weight loss related to cancer-specific treatment.

notes.predicates: Conditions were drafted and reviewed by a language model (model_reviewed), not by clinicians. 'rejected' means the review rejected the draft; the box then needs clinician judgement. 'section_only' means the box only requires the patient to be in the page's guideline section.
notes.coordinates: bbox and line_bboxes are PDF points with the origin at the page's top left; pages[].size gives the page size.
notes.links: page links name a page id from pages[]; a multi-page code such as PROS-F has ids 'PROS-F 1 of 5' ... ; external_guideline links name another guideline's slug.
